title: Neanderthal wooden tools from Spain found preserved in stone
gist: A Science Advances study catalogs 597 wooden remains from Abric Romaní, a Spanish rock shelter where travertine preserved molds of Neanderthal wood, 13 of which were made or modified tools, including a unique club. The finds show routine, planned woodworking and domestic organization, and the lead archaeologist warns that limited time and money may mean similar discoveries are being missed elsewhere.

insights.claim: At Abric Romaní, mineral-rich water coated wooden Neanderthal objects in a limestone-like crust; the wood rotted away and left hollow molds that reproduce its shape, sometimes down to wood-cell outlines, which is rare for Paleolithic wood that otherwise decays quickly.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Shows how an unusual preservation environment can open a data window onto otherwise invisible prehistoric material culture; of little direct market relevance.
insights.quote: These are perfect negatives of the original objects, sometimes so detailed that the outlines of wood cells are visible under a microscope.

insights.claim: The team now digitizes the hollow molds with 3D scanning and photogrammetry and 3D-prints the wooden remains for research and museum displays, replacing the earlier practice of filling hollows with resin or plaster.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: A small example of digital fabrication and scanning becoming standard tooling in archaeology.
insights.quote: Now all the wooden remains are printed in 3D

insights.claim: Most known ancient wooden artifacts are spears from waterlogged sediments where low oxygen slowed decay, so they mainly tell us about hunting rather than daily life.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Explains the sampling bias in the archaeological record that this site corrects.

themes.theme: Scale and composition of the wood sample

insights.claim: Of 597 wooden remains from Neanderthal living areas dated 62,000 to 40,000 years ago, most are natural trunks, branches and firewood (mostly Scots pine), and only 13 were made or modified by Neanderthals.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Gives the base rate: identifiable tools are about 2 percent of recovered wood, so identification is labor-intensive.
insights.quote: Only 13 objects were made or modified by Neanderthals.

insights.claim: Because wooden tools appear level after level across roughly 20,000 years of occupation, woodworking was routine for Neanderthals rather than an occasional one-off, and the tools cover varied subsistence activities, not only hunting.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Supports the view that wood was a core Paleolithic technology we have systematically undercounted.
insights.quote: Because wood turns up in level after level, it shows that woodworking was routine for Neanderthals rather than an occasional one-off.

insights.claim: Juniper-bark trays near hearths, a possible tripod over a hearth, and a pole over five meters long suggest Neanderthals carried food or embers, processed food, and built simple shelters or windbreaks.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Evidence of structured domestic technology argues for greater cognitive and social complexity in Neanderthals.

insights.claim: A row of small hearths along the back wall, present in every excavated level, is interpreted as sleeping hearths that provided light and protection from carnivores.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Interpretive claim about behavior; plausible but hypothesis rather than measured fact.
insights.quote: This gives you illumination and also protects you from possible carnivores or other animals that could attack the group

insights.claim: The shelter has a functional split: a sleeping zone at the back wall and a busier end with overlapping hearths, bones, knapping debris and firewood where food was prepared, tools made, and meals probably shared.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Illustrates spatial planning of living space by Neanderthals.

insights.claim: A pointed stick and two spears were found near red deer skulls, and a cast of the best-preserved 2.45 m spear point shows an impact fracture identical to those on spears used by Aboriginal Australians.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Use-wear evidence ties the spears to actual hunting.

insights.claim: A club carved from a single piece of wood, with a 16 cm handle, a roughly triangular 14 cm head and a right-angle step to stop the hand slipping, has no known parallel; the only earlier suspected club, from Kalambo Falls in Zambia, is about 400,000 years old.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Novel artifact type expands the known Neanderthal toolkit.
insights.quote: According to Chacón, nothing quite like the Romaní club has turned up anywhere.

insights.claim: The club was found in a living area next to bones, stone tools and a hearth, so the team hypothesizes it was used for everyday work rather than ceremony, though Chacón admits they are not sure.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.quote: But when it comes to this club it’s true that we are not sure

insights.claim: Neanderthals chose materials deliberately: easy-to-work, fast-drying Scots pine for cheap replaceable tools, fibrous juniper bark for trays, dry wood for fuel and fresh wood for tools, implying planning and cognitive complexity.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Material selection is evidence of forward planning, a marker of cognitive sophistication.
insights.quote: When they went to look for wood, it was like when they went to look for stone; they knew exactly what they wanted to make

insights.claim: Evidence that Neanderthals twisted fibers into cord, made symbolic objects and interbred with our species is shifting perception away from seeing them as less capable cousins of Homo sapiens.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Part of an ongoing revision of human-evolution narratives.
insights.quote: Neanderthals are no longer perceived as Homo sapiens’ dumb cousins

insights.claim: Studying such tools takes a lot of time and budget: Abric Romaní tools were first described in the 1990s but took decades to identify and catalog, and Chacón worries limited time and funding have caused similar finds elsewhere to be missed.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: A reminder that scientific discovery rates are constrained by funding and labor, not only by availability of material.
insights.quote: To study all these types of tools properly, you need a lot of time and budget

insights.claim: Colleagues report having excavated and photographed possible wood at other sites but not keeping it, and now suspect it could have been a tool, implying discarded evidence.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Suggests archival or re-examination of old excavation records could yield reinterpretations.
insights.quote: perhaps we found something that we thought was wood, we excavated it, we took pictures, but we didn’t keep it
